# The busing project, and why I'm keeping it

Some of you know this from the group chat already. For everyone else, here's the background.

Every fall my juniors in US History II do an oral history project. They find someone in their family or neighborhood who was in Boston between 1974 and 1976 and interview them about busing and desegregation. It's ten minutes of recording and a two-page reflection. I've run it for four years at Cobb Street, two sections a year, and until this fall nobody had complained.

Then a parent emailed Dr. Halvorsen, with a school committee member cc'd, saying the project "reopens wounds" and "pressures kids to judge their grandparents." Halvorsen would like me to quietly drop it. I'm meeting with the two of them next Thursday, the 19th, at 3:15.

I'm not going to drop it.

Jess texted me last night to say, more or less, that it's one assignment and I shouldn't torch my job over it. A fair number of you agreed with her. I started typing a reply and it got so long that I gave up and came here. So this is for all of you, but Jess, it's mostly for you.

First, you're right about the risk. I've had tenure since 2021, so nobody's firing me over a history project. But Halvorsen builds my schedule and decides who gets the AP sections, and there are plenty of ways to make a teacher's year miserable without touching her contract. You taught until 2019 and you do HR for a living now, so you probably know more of those ways than I do. I'm not waving that off. I'm a little scared, honestly. I've been rehearsing Thursday in the shower and I keep losing.

Second, I think the parent has a point, and I want that on the record before anyone imagines me marching into that meeting with a banner. She said the project pressures kids, and it does. If a teacher tells a sixteen-year-old, for a grade, to go ask her grandfather what he was doing in 1975, that's pressure. Some families have very good reasons not to have that conversation at the dinner table because a school said so. I hadn't thought about that as carefully as I should have, and four years without a complaint let me assume I didn't need to.

So the plan I'm bringing Thursday is to keep the project and add another way to do it. A student can interview a librarian or an archivist instead. Or they can work from the interviews past classes recorded, with permission from the people who made them. No kid has to interview anyone in their own family. That's a real change, and I'd have made it years ago if someone had put it to me the way this parent did.

What I won't do is make the whole thing disappear, and the best way to explain why is to tell you about two kids.

In 2023 a student I'll call D. interviewed his grandmother. It turned out she drove a school bus in Southie in 1974. She had never told anyone in the family. Not her kids, nobody. She told D. because he showed up with his phone and a list of questions from his history teacher. He played about forty seconds of the recording for the class, and when it ended nobody said a word for something like a minute. If you've spent time in a room with thirty juniors, you know how rare that is. I've been teaching since you and I were student teachers in 2012 and I can count those silences on one hand.

The other one is harder. Last year a girl in my class found out through her interview that her uncle threw rocks at a bus. She was upset, really upset. We talked after class, twice. That's exactly the scenario the parent's email is worried about, and I won't pretend it was painless. But she wanted to keep going, and the reflection she turned in was the best thing I read all year, from any student, on any assignment.

I think about her when I ask myself if the project is worth it. The kids who get uncomfortable are often the ones getting the most out of it. I believe that. I also believe I don't get to force it on anyone, and that's the line I'm trying to walk. She chose to keep going. With the new option, every kid gets to choose, including choosing not to.

As for "it's one assignment": yes, it is. But our textbook gives busing one paragraph. One paragraph, for something that happened in the city these kids live in, to people they eat Thanksgiving dinner with. If I cut the project, that paragraph is what's left. I'd be teaching Boston kids the history of Boston as though it happened somewhere else, to strangers. I'd also be doing it quietly, because one email went to the right inbox, and I know myself well enough to know the next quiet cut would come easier.

Jess, I don't need you to agree with me. You might read all this and still think I'm being an idiot, and you'd have real evidence on your side. I just want you to know I'm not doing it to be stubborn, and I'm not doing it because I think I'm brave. I've seen what this project does, and I think I can fix the part that's actually wrong with it without throwing out the rest.

I'm not mad about the text, either. You were looking out for me. You've been doing that since we were both 23 and terrified of fourth period.

I'll text you Thursday as soon as I'm out of the meeting, however it goes.

---

One thing to check before you post: I paraphrased Jess's text instead of quoting it, and I avoided a pronoun for Halvorsen since I didn't know which to use.
